paragraphs: Pelimo. Pesahim 8b, 24a; Sanhedrin 10b [Heilprin: 11b]. ‘It was taught: Pelimo says,’ Rosh Hashanah 24a. Yuhasin writes [in Ra'avad's Seder Ha-Kabbalah] that he was Rabbi's colleague. In Menahot 37a he asked Rabbi about a man who has two heads [the Bavli specifies the question was which head should wear tefillin]. He told him: ‘Rise and go into exile, or accept excommunication.’ For it is found in the Zohar, Introduction [Heilprin: Bereshit, עק״פ]: ‘In the place to which Cain was exiled,’ etc., ‘to a place named Arka; all who are born there have two heads.’ End quotation. For that reason he told him, ‘Rise and go into exile,’ meaning to the place where Cain was exiled, and ask that question there; here it is an alien thing, like mockery and ridicule (Tzon Kodashim). Meanwhile a man came whose son had been born with two heads (see Nahum the Elder). ‘It was taught: Pelimo says, “I saw a house that R' Hanina ben Dosa roofed through his prayer [the Bavli attributes the explanation to people who told Pelimo about the house],”’ Ta'anit 25a. Kiddushin 81a–b [Heilprin cites the end of 81a]: Pelimo used to say every day, ‘An arrow in Satan's eyes!’ One day, on the eve of Yom Kippur, he appeared to him as a poor man and called at the door. They brought him bread. He said: ‘On a day like this everyone is inside, and I am outside?’ They brought him in and offered him bread. He said: ‘On a day like this everyone is at the table, and I am alone?’ They seated him at the table. He was covered in boils and sores and behaved disgustingly. They told him: ‘Sit properly.’ He said: ‘Give me a cup.’ They gave him one; he coughed up and cast his phlegm into it. They rebuked him, and he acted as though he had died. They heard people saying, ‘Pelimo killed a man!’ He fled and hid in the privy. Satan went after Pelimo and fell before him. Seeing Pelimo distressed, Satan revealed himself. He asked: ‘Why did you say that?’ (Why did you make a habit of cursing me?) ‘Then how should I speak?’ He told him: ‘Let the master say, “May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.”’ End quotation. Gilgulei Neshamot §112 writes: Pelimo was a spark of Naval; Naval and Lavan are one, and both were stingy. Now they were rectified and came in the pious Pelimo. Satan came to instruct him, to see whether the righteous man would hold to his path as formerly, in stinginess. He presented himself as a poor man and did what he did to see whether he would drive him away, as he had done when he was in the mystery of Naval, who did not wish to give David anything. He used to say ‘An arrow,’ etc., because he recognized his condition and was saying, ‘Let Satan no longer entice me.’ He knew himself to be firmly generous: ‘For you thrust me away; you shall no longer appear to me’ [כ״א דחה דחוני; compact wording retained in sense, reading uncertain]. And behold, ‘he has entirely turned white [lavan]; he is clean.’ They also said that he died at that time during the Ten Days of Repentance—all this for his rectification. In return for the distress he caused Yaakov by pursuing him, Satan now came to distress him, hinting in his words, ‘Have I not distressed you this much?’ He nearly died from fear and dread of the government, because a person had been killed in his house, and he fled until Satan revealed himself to him. See how sweet it is: Lavan plus Naval totals 164; with two units for the two words, it is the numerical value of Pelimo. End quotation.
